title: Counting what can arrive

D0.outcome: Explains that the count on a square can change when more pieces can reach it, and that a target which can move away is a different problem from one that cannot.

D1.outcome: For a stationary target (a pawn that could be pushed or attacked), lists the extra attackers and defenders each side can bring in two moves and states whether the push is safe.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, decides whether to push, support or retreat by comparing arriving reserves, and checks that each would-be defender is not pinned or attackable by a cheaper piece.

D3.outcome: Finds the case where the apparently safe push fails because a single tempo move brings in a third attacker, and names the tempo.

misconceptions: Counting only the pieces already attacking a square.
sources: sources/sheets/edlasker_chess-strategy.md §4 K4, K3, K15; §7 row K4
conditions: The target stays where it is and reinforcements have access to the square.
Each counted reinforcement must be effective: not pinned, not chased away by a cheaper piece.
The count is only the default; a defender can be forced away by a bigger threat.
contrasts: The arrival count favours the pusher, but one of the arriving defenders is attackable by a cheaper piece.
Counting arrivals against a piece that can simply step off the square.
A square no one can reach in the time available.

soft_prereq_notes.TAC.OVERLOAD.D1: a defender forced away is the main way a future count fails
